1289.title: The Sages Who Went to Indra
1289.word: the three doshas as a way of noticing
1289.hook: sick sages send one of their own up to Indra, and he brings back the science of life
1289.carry: health is the root of dharma
1289.tomorrow: a boy fasts fifteen days and forgets his Vedas. why?
1289.howItsDone: Many Hindus see care for the body as part of dharma. Ayurveda, which tradition often links to the Atharva Veda, tells its own beginning as Bharadvaja learning the science of life from Indra for the sake of the sages, and teaches that health is the root of the four aims of life; its dosha clock is used on this path only for noticing.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sushruta's word for well, svastha: health that ends in a clear mind.
screen: `A CLEAR SELF, SENSES AND MIND.`

segments.voice: The Charaka Samhita, one of Ayurveda's oldest texts, opens with a problem, not a cure. Great sages, the story says, had given their lives to prayer, study and self-discipline, and illness kept getting in the way. Bodies gave out before the work was done. So they gathered on a slope of the Himalaya to ask one question: who can help us? And one of them, the sage Bharadvaja, stood up and said: send me.
screen: `A PROBLEM, NOT A CURE.` → `ILLNESS IN THE SAGES' WAY.` → `BHARADVAJA: SEND ME.`

segments.voice: Bharadvaja climbed to Indra, king of the gods, who had received this knowledge, the text says, in a line reaching back to Brahma. Indra taught him the science of life, Ayurveda: ayus, life, and veda, knowledge. He taught it in three parts: the causes of illness, its signs, and what heals. Bharadvaja came back down and taught the sages, and one of them, the teacher Atreya, passed it to six students, one of whom first wrote it down. And here is the line the story is built to deliver. The sages say health is the best root of the four aims of life: dharma, doing what's right; artha, a livelihood; kama, love and joy; and moksha, freedom itself. Illness robs all four. That's a Hindu teaching, said plainly: the body isn't the enemy of the spiritual life, and caring for it isn't vanity. It's the ground the rest grows from. Even the sages needed it. So what does this science see? One verse of the Ashtanga Hridaya, a later classic, gives the doshas a clock: kapha at the beginning, pitta in the middle, vata at the end, of a day, a night, a meal, a whole life. A slow morning may not be a character flaw; some of it may be the hour. On this path that's a way of noticing, never a diagnosis, and anything that keeps on goes to a doctor. And today? The night you skip dinner to study, the week you run on four hours of sleep, the sages would say you're digging up the root.
screen: `INDRA TEACHES BHARADVAJA.` · `HEALTH: THE ROOT OF THE FOUR AIMS.` · `THE BODY IS THE GROUND.` · `KAPHA, THEN PITTA, THEN VATA.`

segments.voice: Sit and feel the body as it is right now: heavy, warm, light or scattered, and notice what part of the day it is. Then, if you pray, thank God for this body, the ground of the four aims, in your own words or a prayer you know. If you don't pray, thank it anyway. It has carried every good thing you've done.
The three doshas, as a way of noticing. Today, the story of how this science came down from Indra, and the line it carries: health is the root of dharma, artha, kama and moksha.
screen: `THE THREE DOSHAS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: health is the root of dharma. Even the sages needed well bodies to pray. See you tomorrow.

1290.title: Fifteen Days of Water
1290.word: the three doshas as a way of noticing
1290.hook: a boy fasts and forgets everything he learned. his father feeds him, and it all comes back
1290.carry: the mind is made of food
1290.tomorrow: where does salt go when it disappears in water?
1290.howItsDone: Many Hindu families offer food to God before eating and receive it as prasad, and some keep simpler, sattvic food on fast days; the Chandogya's 'the mind is made of food' and the Gita's sorting of food by the three gunas stand behind the practice, and Ayurveda's rule that like increases like is used on this path only for noticing.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-NINETY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sages who sent Bharadvaja up to Indra for the science of life: health is the root of dharma.
screen: `HEALTH IS THE ROOT OF DHARMA.`

segments.voice: Shvetaketu has just come home after twelve years of study, and he's rather proud of himself. In the Chandogya Upanishad, his father, Uddalaka, decides to teach him what school didn't. First, a strange test. Don't eat for fifteen days, he says. Drink all the water you like; you won't die, because breath runs on water. Fifteen days later the boy comes back, and his father says: recite the Vedas. Shvetaketu, who knew them all, stands there. Nothing comes. Sir, he says, they don't come to me.
screen: `TWELVE YEARS OF STUDY.` → `FIFTEEN DAYS, ONLY WATER.` → `THE VEDAS DON'T COME.`

segments.voice: His father explains with a picture. Of a great fire, one ember is left, no bigger than a firefly. It can't burn much. Feed it straw, and it blazes up again. Go and eat, he says. Shvetaketu eats, comes back, and recites everything. And Uddalaka gives him the line the story was built for: the mind, my dear, is made of food. Hindu tradition takes that seriously. What goes in becomes you, not only the body but the mind you think and pray with. Later in the same Upanishad: when food is pure, the mind is pure, and when the mind is pure, memory holds firm. Many teachers, Shankara among them, read food there as everything the senses take in. It's why the Gita, in its seventeenth chapter, sorts food by the three gunas: fresh, nourishing, sattvic food that brings strength and contentment; burning, harsh, rajasic food that the Gita says brings pain and grief; stale, spoiled food that suits the dull, tamasic temper. It's why many families offer food to God before they eat it. Ayurveda has a cousin of that logic in one rule from the Charaka Samhita: for all things, at all times, the similar increases and the unlike decreases. Heat on heat stacks up; heavy on heavy. On this path that rule is for noticing what's stacking up, never for prescribing a diet, and health questions go to a doctor. And today? Shvetaketu's ember shows what the night before an exam can forget: you're not only filling a stomach. You're building the mind that has to remember.
screen: `ONE EMBER, LIKE A FIREFLY.` · `THE MIND IS MADE OF FOOD.` · `SATTVIC, RAJASIC, TAMASIC.` · `LIKE INCREASES LIKE.`

segments.voice: At your next meal, if your family offers food first, do it: set the plate down, offer it to God in your heart or with a short prayer you know, then eat it as prasad. If you don't pray, take the first three bites slowly and really taste them, the way Shvetaketu must have after fifteen days. Either way, notice that you're feeding a mind, not just a body.
The three doshas, as a way of noticing. Today, Charaka's rule, like increases like, and the Upanishad's older line underneath it: the mind is made of food.
screen: `THE THREE DOSHAS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the mind is made of food. Feed the ember well, and it blazes. Until tomorrow.

1291.title: The Salt in the Water
1291.word: the three doshas as a way of noticing
1291.hook: a father hides salt in water. his son can't find it anywhere, and can taste it everywhere
1291.carry: tat tvam asi: you are more than your type
1291.tomorrow: Arjuna says the mind is as hard to hold as wind. what does Krishna say?
1291.howItsDone: Ayurvedic practitioners consider both a person's nature (prakriti) and present state (vikriti); in Hindu teaching, from the Chandogya's 'tat tvam asi' onward, the self (atman) is more than either, and students of Vedanta meditate on that line as one of the great sayings. On this path there is no type quiz.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-NINETY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shvetaketu's fast and the line his father drew from it: the mind is made of food.
screen: `THE MIND IS MADE OF FOOD.`

segments.voice: Shvetaketu is still learning from his father. One evening, in the Chandogya Upanishad, Uddalaka hands him a lump of salt. Put this in water, he says, and come to me in the morning. Morning comes: bring me the salt. The boy looks, and can't find it. It's dissolved. Then sip from this end, his father says. Salty. Sip from the middle. Salty. Sip from the far end. Salty. Throw it out, then, and come back. And the boy says what any of us would: it's still there.
screen: `SALT INTO WATER.` → `GONE BY MORNING.` → `SALTY IN EVERY SIP.`

segments.voice: Then Uddalaka says it. You can't see Being here, my dear, but it's here, all through. That finest essence is the self of everything. That's what's real. That is the self. And then the three words Hindus have carried ever since: tat tvam asi. You are that. This is the teaching of atman: under your body, your moods, your habits, there is a self that isn't any of them, and the Upanishad ties it to the Being that runs through everything, like the salt. Hindu schools read just how closely in different ways. Now Ayurveda. Its classical texts ask two questions about a person, and a physician examines both. Prakriti: a person's nature, their constitution, the banks of the river. Vikriti: how things stand now, the water level after a storm. And prakriti is the same word Hindu philosophy uses for nature itself, everything that changes, and the Gita sets it beside the self that knows it. So even Ayurveda's deepest question about you, what's your nature, is a question about the river. Tat tvam asi points to whoever is watching the river. That matters the day someone hands you a label. A quiz says you're pitta, so you're intense, end of story. Hindu teaching would say: you do have a nature, and it's real, and how you are today changes by the afternoon. But you aren't your nature. You are that. On this path there's no type quiz and no diagnosis; that belongs to trained practitioners. What anyone can do is hold the label lightly, and ask how today is.
screen: `TAT TVAM ASI: YOU ARE THAT.` · `PRAKRITI AND VIKRITI: BANKS, WATER.` · `WHO WATCHES THE RIVER?` · `YOU AREN'T YOUR TYPE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the body be as it is today: warm or cool, heavy or light, busy or still. Each time you notice something, say inwardly, I see this. Then rest as the one who sees, the way the salt is in every sip. If you pray, rest in the presence you pray to. If you like, repeat tat tvam asi quietly, a line Vedanta students meditate on.
The three doshas, as a way of noticing. Today, two questions about a person, prakriti and vikriti, and the older answer under both: tat tvam asi, you are that.
screen: `THE THREE DOSHAS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: tat tvam asi, you are more than your type. The salt is in every sip. Same time tomorrow.

1292.title: The Mind Like the Wind
1292.word: the three doshas as a way of noticing
1292.hook: Arjuna tells Krishna the mind can't be held. Krishna agrees, then tells him how
1292.carry: evenness is yoga, and evenness is health
1292.tomorrow: the roosters crow in Dvaraka. what does Krishna do first?
1292.howItsDone: Hindus who meditate often lean on Krishna's answer to Arjuna, practice and letting go, and on his call to moderation in food, sleep and waking; Ayurveda's classical definition of health as the doshas in balance uses the same word, samya, evenness. On this path it is used only for noticing, alongside medical care.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-NINETY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the salt in the water: prakriti and vikriti describe a nature and a day, and tat tvam asi, you are that.
screen: `TAT TVAM ASI.`

segments.voice: On the battlefield, in the sixth chapter of the Gita, Krishna has just described the yogi: still, the mind steady as a lamp in a place with no wind. And Arjuna, honest as ever, pushes back. Krishna, he says, this yoga of evenness you describe, I can't see it lasting. The mind is restless, stormy, strong and stubborn. Holding it seems as hard as holding the wind. It's one of the most human moments in the whole book. And Krishna doesn't tell him he's wrong.
screen: `A LAMP WHERE NO WIND BLOWS.` → `ARJUNA: THE MIND IS LIKE WIND.` → `KRISHNA DOESN'T ARGUE.`

segments.voice: No doubt, Krishna says, the mind is restless and hard to hold. But it can be held, by practice, abhyasa, and by letting go, vairagya. Earlier in the same chapter he's said what that practice looks like day to day. Yoga isn't for the one who eats too much, or not at all; not for the one who sleeps too much, or stays awake too long. It's for the one who is moderate in food and rest, in work, in sleep and waking. Arjuna's word for it was samya, evenness. Earlier, the Gita says it in three words: samatvam yoga uchyate. Evenness is called yoga. Now set a line from the Ashtanga Hridaya beside it: illness is the doshas uneven; health is the doshas even. The same word, samya. Health isn't one dosha driven out. Vata, the moving one, still moves the breath; pitta still digests; kapha still holds you together. It's the three even with each other. And the restless mind Arjuna describes, blowing about like wind? Wind is just what vata means. The spiritual teaching and the medical one meet on the same wire: not the heroic extreme, but evenness, kept by small corrections, again and again. That's the Hindu answer to the all-nighter. The Gita doesn't praise the student who never sleeps; it says that path doesn't hold. Judging an imbalance in the body is a physician's work, and pain, fever or a worrying change goes to a doctor. What Krishna leaves you is the practice: catch the tilt, come back to the middle.
screen: `PRACTICE AND LETTING GO.` · `EVENNESS IS CALLED YOGA.` · `HEALTH: THE THREE DOSHAS EVEN.` · `CATCH THE TILT, COME BACK.`

segments.voice: Sit upright and sway a little left, a little right, each sway smaller, until you settle near the center. Then let the mind rest on one thing. When it blows away like wind, bring it back, as the Gita says, again and again: that is abhyasa. If you pray, rest it on a name of God you love. If you don't, rest it on the breath.
The three doshas, as a way of noticing. Today, one word in two books: samya, evenness. In the Gita it is yoga; in the Ashtanga Hridaya, it is health.
screen: `THE THREE DOSHAS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: evenness is yoga, and evenness is health. Catch the tilt, come back. See you tomorrow.

1293.title: Krishna's Morning in Dvaraka
1293.hook: the queens curse the roosters for crowing. Krishna gets up and keeps an ordinary morning, on purpose
1293.carry: the ordinary morning is part of dharma
1293.tomorrow: a sage wakes two princes in the dark. what is waiting?
1293.howItsDone: Many Hindus bathe and put on clean clothes before the morning puja, then light a lamp and pray; Ayurveda's dinacharya (cleaning the teeth, scraping the tongue, oil, bath) runs alongside, and the Bhagavata's account of Krishna's morning in Dvaraka is one picture of that ordinary, sacred round.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-NINETY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Arjuna's mind like the wind, and Krishna's answer: evenness is yoga, and the doshas' evenness is health.
screen: `EVENNESS IS YOGA.`

segments.voice: Dvaraka, before dawn. In the Bhagavata Purana the roosters start crowing, and Krishna's queens curse them, because the crowing means he's about to leave their side. The roosters don't care. Krishna gets up. And then the text does something you might not expect in a story about God. It walks through his morning, step by step. He touches water. He sits in silent meditation. He bathes, puts on clean clothes, and does his morning prayers and offerings, repeating a sacred mantra in silence, before he sees anyone at all.
screen: `THE ROOSTERS CROW.` → `THE QUEENS CURSE THEM.` → `KRISHNA GETS UP.`

segments.voice: Then he greets the rising sun, honors his elders, gives gifts, and only after that turns to the business of the day. Why spend all those words on God's morning? One answer comes from Krishna himself, in the Gita: whatever the great do, others follow. If I didn't keep to my work, people everywhere would follow my lead. So the Lord keeps an ordinary morning, on purpose. That's the teaching: in Hindu life the ordinary morning is part of dharma, not the boring part before it. Many homes still keep its shape: a bath before worship, clean clothes, then the lamp and a prayer. The Yoga Sutra names cleanness, shaucha, first among the observances it asks for. Ayurveda gives the same morning its own name: dinacharya. Dina, day; charya, conduct; the day's conduct. The Charaka Samhita's chapter on daily regimen starts with eating in the right measure, then walks through things anyone would recognize: caring for the eyes, cleaning the teeth with a twig, scraping the tongue, rinsing the mouth, oil for the body, a bath, clean clothes. One text calls this health; the other calls it dharma. They keep the same hours. And today? It's easy to treat the morning as something to get through before life starts. Krishna's story says the morning is where the day is first offered. The toothbrush counts. The shower before the prayer counts.
screen: `WHAT THE GREAT DO, OTHERS FOLLOW.` · `THE MORNING IS PART OF DHARMA.` · `DINACHARYA: THE DAY'S CONDUCT.` · `ONE MORNING: HEALTH AND DHARMA.`

segments.voice: Picture tomorrow morning, step by step: water, the sink, the shower, clean clothes. If you pray, choose one of those ordinary acts and offer it to God before you do it, the way a bath comes before puja. If you don't pray, choose one and decide now to do it slowly and on purpose, the way the Bhagavata walks through Krishna's.
The daily routine. Dinacharya, the day's conduct: the morning round of the Ayurvedic texts, kept in Hindu homes beside the bath, the lamp and the first prayer.

1294.title: Rise, Rama: The Dawn Has Come
1294.hook: a sage wakes two princes by a river in the dark. temples still sing his words to wake God every dawn
1294.carry: the day begins with the sacred
1294.tomorrow: a boy asks Death what comes after. why does Death draw him a chariot?
1294.howItsDone: Many Hindus rise in brahma muhurta for prayer, look at their palms on waking and say 'karagre vasate Lakshmi', or play the Venkateshwara Suprabhatam, which opens with Vishvamitra's words to Rama and is sung before dawn at Tirumala; Ayurvedic texts also recommend waking then for a person in health.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-NINETY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Krishna's morning in Dvaraka: water, a bath, clean clothes, prayer. The ordinary morning is part of dharma.
screen: `EVEN KRISHNA KEPT A MORNING.`

segments.voice: Two young princes are asleep on a bed of grass beside a river, a long way from the palace. Rama and his brother Lakshmana have left home with the sage Vishvamitra, and this is their first night out. In the Ramayana, as the night ends, the sage leans over the sleeping boys and wakes them with a verse. Rama, blessed son of Kausalya, the eastern twilight is beginning. Get up, tiger among men. The day's rites to the gods are waiting.
screen: `TWO PRINCES ON A BED OF GRASS.` → `THE SAGE LEANS OVER THEM.` → `RISE, RAMA. THE DAWN HAS COME.`

segments.voice: The boys get up, bathe, say their morning prayers, bow to their teacher, and walk on. It's a small scene in a long epic. But those two lines became the opening of the Venkateshwara Suprabhatam, the hymn sung before dawn at the great temple at Tirumala to wake the Lord, and played at sunrise in many Hindu homes. The words a sage used to wake a prince are used to wake God, and the household wakes with him. That's the teaching: in Hindu life, the day begins with the sacred. The time just before sunrise even has a name, brahma muhurta, prized for prayer, study and meditation. Ayurveda's Ashtanga Hridaya opens its daily routine right there: a healthy person should rise in brahma muhurta, to protect their life. And many families keep a tiny prayer for the very first waking moment. You look at your open palms and say: at the tips of the hands lives Lakshmi, in the middle Sarasvati, at the base Govinda; so at dawn, look at your hands. Wealth, learning and God, in the hands you're about to use all day. Now think where most hands go first: to a glowing screen, and the day arrives from somewhere else. Vishvamitra's verse and the palm prayer turn that around. Not everyone can rise in the dark, a new parent, a night-shift worker, someone who's sick; the verse speaks to the healthy. But anyone can give the first minute to something holy before the phone gets it.
screen: `KAUSALYA SUPRAJA RAMA.` · `THE DAY BEGINS WITH THE SACRED.` · `KARAGRE VASATE LAKSHMI.` · `THE FIRST MINUTE, BEFORE THE PHONE.`

segments.voice: Try the palm prayer now, the way many families do on waking. Open your hands and look at them: fingertips, palms, the base of the palm. If you pray, say the verse, karagre vasate Lakshmi, or just its meaning: Lakshmi, Sarasvati, Govinda, in these hands. If you don't, look anyway and ask what these hands will do today. Tomorrow, try looking at them before the phone.

1295.title: The Chariot and the Horses
1295.hook: a boy asks Death what comes after, and Death answers with a chariot pulled by the senses
1295.carry: the self rides; the senses are the horses
1295.tomorrow: why do families bathe in oil before dawn on Diwali?
1295.howItsDone: Many Hindus learn the Katha Upanishad's chariot as a picture of self-mastery, the senses as horses guided by understanding; people who follow Ayurveda's morning round tend the eyes, clean the teeth, scrape the tongue, rinse the mouth, and some oil the body before bathing.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-NINETY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vishvamitra woke Rama at dawn, and the palm prayer still begins many Hindu mornings: the day begins with the sacred.
screen: `HANDS BEFORE THE PHONE.`

segments.voice: In the Katha Upanishad, a boy named Nachiketa goes to the house of Death and waits three nights at the door without food, because Death isn't home. When Yama, the lord of death, returns, he's dismayed to have left a guest unfed, and offers the boy three wishes. For the third, Nachiketa asks the question Yama would rather not answer: what happens to a person after death? Yama tries to buy him off with long life, riches and pleasures. Keep them, says the boy. So Death teaches him, and in the middle of the teaching, he draws a picture.
screen: `THREE NIGHTS AT DEATH'S DOOR.` → `THREE WISHES.` → `KEEP YOUR RICHES. TELL ME.`

segments.voice: Know the self, says Yama, as the rider in a chariot, and the body as the chariot. The intellect is the driver. The mind is the reins. The senses are the horses, and the things they want are the roads. A driver who doesn't understand, reins slack, has horses that run wild. A driver who understands, reins in hand, has horses that go where he's headed. That's a central Hindu teaching about the senses, the indriyas: they aren't enemies to kill. They're strong, good horses that need a steady driver. The Gita says it with another animal: the steady person draws the senses back from what pulls at them, the way a tortoise draws in its limbs. Now look again at the morning care the Ayurvedic texts describe. The eyes are tended. The teeth are cleaned with a twig. The tongue is scraped, the mouth rinsed. Oil for the body, then a bath. Eyes, tongue, mouth, skin: each horse is groomed before the ride. Read with Yama's picture, the morning round isn't only hygiene. It's the driver checking the team before taking the road. And today? The horses get pulled a hundred ways before breakfast: a buzz, a glow, a smell, a scroll. Hindu teaching doesn't ask you to blind the horses. It asks who's holding the reins. So the week ends where it began, with Indra's sages: the body is the chariot that carries the self.
screen: `THE SELF RIDES; THE MIND, THE REINS.` · `THE SENSES: STRONG, GOOD HORSES.` · `EACH HORSE GROOMED BEFORE THE RIDE.` · `WHO'S HOLDING THE REINS?`

segments.voice: Sit, and check the team. The eyes: light and shape. The ears: the nearest sound, then the farthest. The nose, the taste in your mouth, the skin: clothes, air, the weight where you sit. Don't chase anything; let each horse settle. Then gather them in, the way the tortoise draws in its limbs, and rest in the breath. If you pray, offer the whole ride to God; Yama says the good driver reaches the end of the road, the highest place of Vishnu.
The daily routine. In the classical morning, eyes, teeth, tongue, mouth and skin are tended in turn, and Yama's chariot shows why: the senses are the horses.
